questionStem: During transfusion of a second unit of crossmatched packed red blood cells, a 62-year-old man has the sudden onset of fever, chills, and mild shortness of breath . Transfusion of the first unit was completed 1 hour ago. Yesterday, he underwent a left hemicolectomy for colon cancer. His temperature is 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), pulse is 90/min , and blood pressure is 126/77 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation . The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . A direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is negative . Urinalysis shows no hemoglobin . Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
correctExplanation: Transfusion reactions can range from mild (e.g., itching, fever, mild rash) to severe (e.g., hemolysis, anaphylaxis). Most reactions are mild and do not necessitate the cessation of a transfusion. An acute febrile transfusion reaction (febrile, non hemolytic transfusion reaction [FNHTR]) occurs because of the presence of preformed antibodies to donor leukocyte antigens and occasionally from cytokines in the plasma component of the transfused sample. FNHTR ranges from mild (mild fever, minimal additional symptoms) to severe (high fevers, rigors, myalgias, nausea). Treatment consists of pausing the transfusion to rule out ABO incompatibility or a severe reaction such as transfusion-related acute lung injury and administering antipyretics. FNHTR can be prevented through leukoreduction of transfused blood.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction (AHTR) (Choice A) results from a mismatch between donor and recipient blood groups, caused by native recipient immunoglobulins against the donor antigen. AHTR can be life­ threatening because of hemolysis, end-stage kidney disease, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), and hypotension. Diagnosis is based on the history and laboratory workup for hemolysis plus type mismatch; treatment begins with immediate discontinuation of the transfusion. Anaphylactic transfusion reaction (Choice B) occurs when transfused blood contains an antigen against which the recipient has preformed lgE antibodies, leading to a rapid and severe type I (immediate) hypersensitivity reaction with diffuse mast cell degranulation and histamine release. Symptoms include flushing, itching, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, bronchospasm, shortness of breath, angioedema, and in severe cases, airway obstruction and distributive shock. Classically, anaphylactic transfusion reactions are seen in recipients with lgA deficiency when they receive lgA fragments in donated blood. Delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction (DHTR) (Choice C) occurs because of the recipient developing antibodies against donor antigens generally occurring 1 to 10 days following transfusion. Hemolysis, with resultant anemia, jaundice, and fatigue may occur. In general, DHTR symptoms are much milder than the symptoms of AHTR, and end-stage kidney disease, DIC, and hypotension are less common. Transfusion-related acute lung injury (Choice E) generally occurs within 6 hours of a blood transfusion. It is a serious complication that is characterized by noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. Symptoms include fever, dyspnea, severe hypoxemia, and shock. It more frequently occurs following a transfusion of platelets or plasma and is hypothesized to be immune-mediated. " , ~ F' r ,

questionStem: A 72-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of right-sided upper abdominal pain; he has had decreased appetite resulting in a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss during this period. He has consumed 4 ounces of whiskey daily for 50 years . He is 193 cm (6 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 82 kg (180 lb); BMI is 22 kg/m 2• His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), and blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows no abnormalities . Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit Mean corpuscular volume Serum Bilirubin , total Direct Alkaline phosphatase AST Lactate dehydrogenase Lipase 38% 90 µm3 2 mg/dL 1.4 mg/dL 500 U/L 50 U/L 200 U/L 42 U/L (N=14-280) Abdominal ultrasonography shows dilated intrahepatic ducts in both lobes and a small gallbladder . A CT scan of the abdomen shows no additional abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.A: Measurement of serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) concentration

correctExplanation: Cholangiocarcinoma, a malignancy of the bile ducts, characteristically presents late in its course with signs of biliary tree obstruction, including abdominal discomfort, weight loss, nausea, jaundice, and pruritus. Patients may report dark urine or light, pale stools. Many persons have no risk factors; however, those with a history of cirrhosis, sclerosing cholangitis, hepatitis B or C, liver fluke infection, and ulcerative colitis may be at increased risk. Diagnosis occurs through imaging of the abdomen with CT scan or MRI, which may disclose a variety of findings from bile duct wall thickening, a focal mass, or only dilation of bile ducts proximal to the presumed lesion location. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) allows for the potential direct visualization of the lesion location, bile duct scrapings or biopsy for definitive diagnosis, and stenting of any associated occlusion. Laboratory analysis typically discloses obstructive (direct) hyperbilirubinemia and increased alkaline phosphatase activity. Treatment includes surgical resection and chemotherapy; however, the condition is often late-stage or terminal at the time of diagnosis.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Measurement of serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) concentration (Choice A) is sometimes increased in cholangiocarcinoma; however, it is nonspecific and is also increased in colorectal carcinoma along with other various malignancies. It may be followed during treatment to assess treatment response but does not have a specific role in diagnosis. Hepatobiliary scintigraphy (HIDA scan) (Choice C) evaluates the patency of the hepatobiliary tree and gallbladder. It is useful in cases of suspected acute cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, or biliary obstruction with indeterminate ultrasonography findings. It does not permit tissue sampling such as biopsy or therapeutic interventions such as stenting. Liver biopsy (Choice D) is useful in the diagnosis of conditions such as cirrhosis, hepatitis, and hepatocellular carcinoma, though cholangiocarcinoma is generally small and confined to the biliary tree. These features may result in false negative liver biopsy results and should prompt targeted sampling via ERCP. Exploratory laparotomy (Choice E) involves the surgical evaluation of the peritoneal cavity and is commonly employed in the diagnosis and management of abdominal trauma, bowel obstruction, peritonitis, and undifferentiated cases of an acute abdomen. It does not have an immediate role in the diagnosis or management of cholangiocarcinoma. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department after being stabbed in the anterior neck 30 minutes ago. Examination shows a large, pulsatile hematoma at the level of the thyroid cartilage . As the physician watches , the hematoma expands . Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?

choices.A: Esophagoscopy to rule out esophageal injury

correctExplanation: The initial evaluation of a critically ill patient includes assessing the airway, breathing, circulation, central nervous system, and any external threats to morbidity or mortality. The initial airway assessment determines whether the patient is at risk for compromise to the pathway of airflow from the external environment into the lungs. Examples of airway compromise include structural lesions (angioedema, facial or neck trauma, airway foreign bodies, expanding neck hematomas), space-filling lesions (pharyngeal, laryngeal, tracheal, or bronchial hemorrhage), uncontrolled emesis, or loss of airway protective reflexes (altered mental status). Airway management requires immediate priority whenever a compromising lesion is detected, and an expanding neck hematoma under arterial pressure (pulsatile) may threaten the pathway of airflow within minutes. Endotracheal intubation is the best next step to ensure an intact pathway for air exchange.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Esophagoscopy to rule out esophageal injury (Choice A) may be necessary in the evaluation of a penetrating neck trauma; however, it should follow emergent management of the airway, breathing, and circulation, as it is a less immediate threat. Arteriography (Choice C) may be indicated to assess damage to the carotid arteries or their branches; however, in an unstable patient with an expanding, pulsatile neck hematoma, securing the airway and empirically controlling bleeding are earlier priorities. Additionally, zone two neck injuries are generally managed by direct exploration, whereas zone one and zone three injuries are managed first with vessel imaging before operative exploration. Cricothyroidotomy (Choice D) and tracheostomy (Choice E) may be indicated in cases of airway compromise in which endotracheal intubation is unsuccessful. However, in cases of an expanding, arterial neck hematoma, these maneuvers may be difficult or impossible depending on the location of the hematoma. Additionally, inadvertent decompression of an arterial hematoma in the neck may result in exsanguination along with additional airway compromise via hemorrhage into the newly created ostomy. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 57-year-old woman has had pain of the left groin and distal anterior thigh with weight bearing for 3 months . She has difficulty bending forward and tying her left shoe. She walks with a mild limp favoring her left lower extremity. Internal rotation of the left hip produces pain. There is no tenderness over the lateral thigh. Muscle strength and deep tendon reflexes are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Osteoarthritis is a noninflammatory arthropathy that occurs secondary to deterioration of articular cartilage. It typically occurs in older persons and may affect any joint. It is commonly associated with the fingers and wrists because of repetitive use, and the hips and knees because of chronic weight bearing, especially in persons with obesity. It is not associated with infectious or inflammatory symptoms and is generally insidious in onset. Patients typically report chronic pain in a joint that is worse with movement or exertion and is improved with rest, often with limited range of motion in a joint because of underlying joint space narrowing and associated pain. Fever, chills, erythema over a joint, traumatic injury, or extra-articular manifestations (e.g., rashes, uveitis, urethritis) suggest an alternate, inflammatory, or infectious cause. Imaging may demonstrate osteophytosis, subchondral cystic or sclerotic changes, and space narrowing of joints. Arthrocentesis typically demonstrates leukocytes of less than 2,000/mm 3 with no additional abnormalities. Treatment includes rest, physical therapy, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, intra-articular injections (e.g., cortisone), and joint replacement surgery for severe or refractory cases.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Lumbar radiculopathy (Choice A) presents with pain that radiates down the leg along a specific dermatome secondary to impingement or stretching of a lumbar nerve root, and it often results from underlying degenerative changes of the lumbar spine. It is classically worse with a straight-leg raise maneuver, which stretches the lumbar root and elicits radicular pain, often described as "shooting down the leg." Osteoarthritis of the knee (Choice C) is common in older persons and those with obesity. Pain with osteoarthritis of the knee classically occurs in the knee joint itself and would be unlikely to radiate to the groin or thigh. It may also be associated with knee joint instability. Rheumatoid arthritis of the hip (Choice D) typically is worse in the morning (after a period of rest) with prolonged joint stiffness and improves with use. Extra-articular manifestations of rheumatoid arthritis may also be present such as rheumatoid nodules, pulmonary fibrosis, vasculitis, Sjogren syndrome, and dermatologic manifestations. Trochanteric bursitis (Choice E) presents with localized pain and swelling, often with overlying erythema in the area of the affected bursa. A common risk factor is prolonged pressure applied to the bursa. The associated pain generally does not radiate. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 40-year-old woman comes to the physician for a follow-up examination . She recently tested positive for the BRCA 1 mutation . She wishes to discuss treatment options . She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications . Her mother and a sister were diagnosed with breast cancer at the ages of 39 and 43 years , respectively . Another sister was diagnosed with breast and ovarian cancer at the age of 35 years . Examination and mammography of the patient show no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management to decrease this patient's risk for developing a BRCA-associated cancer?

choices.C: Tamoxifen therapy and bilateral mastectomy and oophorectomy

correctExplanation: BRCA 1, a hereditary tumor suppressor gene, is highly associated with the development of breast and ovarian malignancies when it is nonfunctional, suppressed, or subfunctional. BRCA 1 expression is low in the majority of high-grade, ductal breast and epithelial ovarian cancers. BRCA 1 plays an important role in the repair of double-stranded DNA breaks, and absent or low-expression of this protein promotes mutations which may eventually lead to malignancy. In families with a strong history of early breast and/or ovarian malignancy, with a known BRCA 1 mutation, the risk for breast or ovarian cancer in women can be decreased through a bilateral mastectomy and oophorectomy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Tamoxifen therapy and bilateral mastectomy (Choice B) and tamoxifen therapy and bilateral oophorectomy (Choice D) would limit the patient's risk for either breast cancer or ovarian cancer, respectively, but would still present an increased risk for additional BRCA-associated cancers. Tamoxifen has been shown to reduce the risk for developing breast cancer, but to a lesser extent than prophylactic mastectomy. Tamoxifen therapy and bilateral mastectomy and oophorectomy (Choice C) would not offer additional preventive benefit as compared to isolated surgical removal, as once the organs are no longer present, the risk for malignancy is minimized provided a complete resection occurred. Tamoxifen therapy only (Choice E) may reduce the risk for breast cancer but has been hypothesized to increase the risk for ovarian cancer through the development of ovarian cysts. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: An 82-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital because she has refused to eat because of a 2-day history of severe abdominal pain. She has type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with insulin. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 102/min, and blood pressure is 110/85 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows mild, diffuse tenderness to palpation . Serum studies show: Na• 138 mEq/L K+ 4 mEq/L Cl- 103 mEq/L HCO3- 20 mEq/L Glucose 202 mg/dl A CT scan of the abdomen shows thickening of the wall of the small bowel. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Mesenteric ischemia can be acute or chronic. The acute form is often associated with thrombosis or embolism involving the superior or inferior mesenteric arteries, and it classically presents with severe abdominal pain out of proportion to examination, nausea, vomiting, hematochezia, and potentially signs of peritonitis. Laboratory evaluation often discloses leukocytosis and an increased lactate concentration. Imaging may demonstrate thickening of the bowel wall along with pneumatosis intestinalis and possible portal venous gas or pneumoperitoneum. Chronic mesenteric ischemia occurs because of atherosclerotic narrowing of the mesenteric arteries, which impairs intestinal blood flow during times of increased demand such as following a meal. Patients are typically food averse and may present with chronic weight loss. Diagnosis of mesenteric ischemia, both acute and chronic, requires mesenteric angiography, which will evaluate the patency of the mesenteric arteries and allow for therapeutic intervention with thrombectomy, embolectomy, angioplasty, or stenting.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Infusion of heparin {Choice A) is appropriate in cases of splenic, portal, hepatic, or mesenteric vein thrombosis, which would cause upstream vascular congestion. Initiation of heparin therapy is appropriate for the management of mesenteric ischemia once a diagnosis has been established. Intravenous administration of dopamine {Choice B) is used in cases of cardiogenic shock or refractory hypotension. It may theoretically prevent splanchnic vasoconstriction because of D1 and D2 receptor agonism; however, this has not been demonstrated in clinical practice. Colonoscopy {Choice C) is useful in the diagnosis and management of colorectal pathology such as malignancy, inflammatory bowel disease, arteriovenous malformation, and strictures. It does not have an immediate role in the diagnosis or management of acute mesenteric ischemia. Esophagoduodenostomy {Choice E) creates an anastomosis between the esophagus and duodenum for reconstruction following gastrectomy. It does not have an immediate role in the diagnosis or management of mesenteric ischemia. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 36-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus has fever and flank pain. Her temperature is 39°C (102.2°F). Gram stain of the urinary sediment shows many segmented neutrophils and gram-negative bacilli. Leukocyte count is 27,000/mm 3 with 80% segmented neutrophils and 5% bands. Urine culture is positive for Escherichia coli. Ampicillin and gentamicin are administered intravenously . Ten days later, she continues to be febrile . Which of the following is the most likely cause?

choices.C: Natural course of E. coli pyelonephritis in a diabetic patient

correctExplanation: Perinephric abscess is a potential complication of pyelonephritis and may result from untreated, persistent, or treatment-refractory disease, often presenting with recurrent or persistent symptoms after antibiotic therapy. Pyelonephritis occurs because of the retrograde spread of a lower urinary tract infection. Urinary tract infections are more common in women because of the shorter urethra and favorable regional environment for bacterial growth and in persons with diabetes mellitus because of the presence of glucosuria. Upper urinary tract infections such as pyelonephritis and perinephric abscess more commonly present with systemic symptoms such as rigors, nausea, vomiting, myalgias, arthralgias, fatigue, high fevers, tachycardia, leukocytosis, flank pain, and costovertebral angle tenderness on physical examination. Urinalysis in pyelonephritis and perinephric abscess often shows greater than 10 WBC/hpf and may show WBC casts. Bacteria are generally seen on microscopy, with gram-negative rods (especially Escherichia coll) being the most common pathogen. Pyelonephritis complicated by perinephric abscess should be treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics and may require surgical or percutaneous drainage for source control.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Development of antibiotic resistance {Choice A) cannot be excluded in the setting of pyelonephritis or perinephric abscess. However, it would typically present with recurrent symptoms following improvement as opportunistic bacteria gain the opportunity for reinfection. Persistent infection or an absence of improvement suggests suboptimal treatment because of failed antibiotic penetration of an abscess cavity. Drug reaction {Choice B) may present with initial allergic or anaphylactic symptoms, which may include itching, rash, angioedema, shortness of breath, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or shock. Delayed drug reactions include syndromes such as acute interstitial nephritis, which presents with rash, fever, acute kidney injury, and sterile eosinophiluria. Natural course of E. coli pyelonephritis in a diabetic patient {Choice C) is incorrect as the typical course of pyelonephritis in a person with diabetes mellitus that is controlled includes improvement generally within 2 to 3 days of antibiotic treatment. Even in cases of poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, antibiotics, fluids, and supportive care will generally eradicate the infection within 3 to 5 days unless complicating features (e.g., perinephric abscess) are present. Splenic infarct {Choice E) presents with left upper quadrant abdominal pain and would not present with pyuria or positive urine cultures. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 42-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 45 minutes after being involved in a motor vehicle collision . She was the restrained driver. On arrival, she has severe abdominal pain. Her temperature is 36.5°C (97. 7°F), pulse is 92/min , respirations are 13/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. There is an abrasion over the right flank . The abdomen is nondistended with severe right upper quadrant tenderness . The remainder of the examination , including pelvic and rectal examination , shows no abnormalities . Her hemoglobin concentration is 10.5 g/dl . There is gross hematuria . A pelvic x-ray shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Blunt abdominal trauma (BAT) in the setting of hemodynamic stability is best evaluated using a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis. BAT is commonly associated with injury involving the liver, spleen, and kidneys, and can include hematomas, contusions, lacerations, and in severe cases, devascularization and uncontrolled hemorrhage. Hematuria is highly suggestive of renal or retroperitoneal bleeding or hematoma. In contrast to stable BAT, hemodynamically unstable BAT is evaluated first with focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) followed by an exploratory laparotomy if positive, whereas stable BAT permits time for more thorough evaluation and the additional detail offered in a CT scan. Patients should also receive intravenous fluids, pain control, and supportive care as needed. There should be close monitoring of the patient's hemodynamics, as decompensation may occur rapidly if bleeding is present or continues unabated.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Measurement of serum creatinine concentration (Choice A) has a role in the evaluation of renal function following BAT but would not have an immediate role in the evaluation of a traumatic renal injury until such an injury is identified on a CT scan. Cystography (Choice C) and cystoscopy (Choice E) have roles in the workup of hematuria when a bladder source is suspected. Retrograde urethrography (Choice D) permits evaluation of the urethra as a source of hematuria. However, in undifferentiated cases of BAT, a CT scan permits evaluation of the liver, spleen, kidneys, ureters, retroperitoneum, bladder, bony pelvis, and prostate, and should precede dedicated bladder or urethral imaging. Exploratory laparotomy (Choice F) is the correct choice in the management of unstable BAT, as it permits the control of hemorrhage and the repair of identified injuries. In stable cases, imaging precedes surgical intervention. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A previously healthy 6-year-old girl is admitted to the hospital because of a 2-day history of fever and progressive left hip pain. She has refused to bear weight on her left leg since awakening 4 hours ago. There is no history of trauma . She is now lying on the stretcher with her left leg abducted and externally rotated . Her temperature is 39.1 °C (102.4 °F), pulse is 130/min, respirations are 24/min , and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. On examination , she resists any motion of the left lower extremity. There is warmth over the left hip but no erythema or swelling . Her erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 70 mm/h. Arthrocentesis of the left hip yields cloudy fluid; joint fluid analysis shows an erythrocyte count of 1 0,000/mm 3 and leukocyte count of 196,000/mm 3. Results of culture of the synovial fluid are pending . X-rays of the pelvis and left lower extremity show no abnormalities . In addition to intravenous antibiotic therapy, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.D: Daily needle aspiration of the hip until her symptoms resolve

correctExplanation: Septic arthritis is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus and presents with pain, inability to bear weight, reduced range of motion, fever, chills, nausea, myalgias, arthralgias, and fatigue. Vital signs may disclose a fever, tachycardia, or hypotension if it is complicated by bacteremia or sepsis. Physical examination typically discloses tenderness to palpation of the affected joint, a limited range of motion, pain with range of motion, joint effusion, and overlying cutaneous erythema. Routes of infection include direct inoculation, spread from an adjacent infection such as osteomyelitis, or hematogenous seeding. Diagnosis is through physical examination plus arthrocentesis, which classically discloses a neutrophilic-predominant exudate with a leukocyte count greater than 50,000/mm 3• Organisms are often seen on Gram stain and are detected by culture. Treatment includes intravenous antibiotics plus emergent surgical incision and drainage to prevent complications including articular erosion, fibrous ankylosis, loss of the ability to ambulate, and the potential for sepsis and even death if severe.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Aspirin therapy (Choice A) is appropriate for cases of musculoskeletal pain or inflammatory arthritis but is generally never appropriate for use in a child outside of mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome (Kawasaki disease) because of the risk for Reye syndrome. It does not have a defined role in the management of septic arthritis. Colchicine therapy (Choice B) is appropriate for inflammatory arthritis and is classically used in the treatment of gout. It inhibits microtubule formation which prevents white blood cell translocation into the joint, limiting inflammation and resultant arthropathy. Prednisone therapy (Choice C) is used primarily for inflammatory arthritis and has a role in the management of rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus-associated arthritis, and seronegative spondyloarthropathies. Daily needle aspiration of the hip until her symptoms resolve (Choice D) would not appropriately resolve the infection. Emergent surgical incision and drainage followed by antibiotics are required to prevent joint complications and potential sepsis. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 37-year-old man comes to the physician because of bilateral breast enlargement for 6 months. He takes no medications and does not drink alcohol. Examination shows tender gynecomastia bilaterally and a small nodule on the left testicle . Liver function tests and serum 13-hCG concentration are within the reference range . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Leydig cell tumors arise from the interstitial cells of the testicle, specifically the Leydig cell, which physiologically produces sex hormones in response to stimulus from luteinizing hormone. Generally, Leydig cells secrete androgens in men; however, they can also secrete estrogens, especially in states of dysregulation (e.g., malignancy). In young boys, such upregulation of androgens presents with precocious puberty, while in women it presents with masculinization (e.g., amenorrhea, hirsutism, temporal balding, acne, deepening of the voice, clitoromegaly). Gynecomastia and a testicular nodule in a postpubertal, otherwise healthy male is suggestive of a functional estrogen­ secreting Leydig cell tumor. Diagnosis requires testicular ultrasonography, followed by orchiectomy and histologic evaluation.
incorrectExplanation: nd J. Chancroid (Choice A) presents with an exudative painful genital ulcer with inguinal lymphadenopathy and is caused by infection from Haemophi/us ducreyi. It does not cause testicular nodules or gynecomastia. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) (Choice B) defines a variable state of disease related to adrenal hypofunction that results in decreased concentrations of cortisol with variable effects on mineralocorticoids and androgens. The presentation varies depending on the age of onset, severity, and gender of the patient. In rare, mild cases, infertility may be the only presenting symptom when declared in adolescence or young adulthood. Most cases of CAH are diagnosed in childhood. Testicular nodules are not a presenting feature. Epididymitis (Choice C) is a common cause of painful scrotal swelling and refers to acute infection and inflammation of the epididymis. In younger males, this is commonly secondary to sexually transmitted infections such as Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae. In older males, Escherichia coli is more common. Herpes simplex (Choice D) presents with painful genital lesions that begin as areas of erythema, erupt as clear, fluid-filled, confluent vesicles, and subsequently evolve to crusted ulcerations which heal without leaving a scar. Hydroceles (Choice E) occur because of the presence of a patent tunica vaginal is. They are fluid-filled sacs within the scrotum, are nontender, non-nodular, and transilluminate on examination. Gynecomastia is not a feature of the condition. Penile cancer (Choice G) is rare, but when present is often squamous cell carcinoma. Risk factors include a lack of circumcision and infection with human papillomavirus. Precursor lesions to cancer of the penis are Bowen disease, which presents as leukoplakia of the penile shaft, or erythroplasia of Queyrat, which presents as erythroplakia of the glans. Pituitary adenoma (Choice H) is associated with gynecomastia and galactorrhea when prolactin is functionally produced by the tumor; however, a prolactinoma would not present with a testicular nodule. Typical signs of a pituitary tumor include features related to its mass effect in the sella turcica with loss of other pituitary hormones, or damage to the optic chiasm resulting in bitemporal hemianopsia on examination. Primary gonadal failure (Choice I) presents in men with the failure to develop secondary sexual characteristics during puberty, including decreased body hair, low muscle mass, erectile dysfunction, infertility, gynecomastia, and small testes. Syphilis (Choice J) demonstrates multiple stages with varying symptoms, including primary with a painless chancre, secondary with fever, lymphadenopathy, and condylomata lata, and tertiary with tabes dorsalis, aortitis, and gummas. The painless chancre of primary syphilis can present as a painless ulcerative genital lesion and would not classically present with a testicular nodule or gynecomastia. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: Thirty minutes after undergoing a radical gastrectomy for gastric carcinoma , a 67-year-old woman has an oxygen saturation of 84%. She was extubated in the operating room and is currently receiving 6 L/min of oxygen via nasal cannula and intravenous morphine for pain. She has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 50 years and has mild chronic obstructive pulmonary disease . Her temperature is 38°C (100.4°F), pulse is 105/min and regular, respirations are 11/min, and blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg. There is no jugular venous distention . Breath sounds are decreased at the bases. Cardiac examination shows no murmurs or gallops . A portable x-ray of the chest shows moderate elevation of both diaphragms ; no other abnormalities are noted. Arterial blood gas analysis shows : Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this patient's respiratory insufficiency?
correctExplanation: 7.26 73 mm Hg 56 mm Hg 29 mEq/L Following thoracic or abdominal surgery, breathing often creates discomfort for patients by exacerbating postoperative pain. As a result, patients often splint their breathing, resulting in bradypnea and low tidal volume, which will decrease alveolar minute ventilation leading to the development of hypoxemia and acute respiratory acidosis. Underlying respiratory impairment (e.g., history of smoking, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) may further exacerbate hypoventilation. Vital signs may disclose bradypnea and low arterial oxygen saturation. Physical examination will demonstrate diminished respiratory effort, often with reduced breath sounds at the lung bases because of atelectasis and inadequate diaphragmatic excursion. Arterial blood gas analysis may disclose an acidic pH with increases in both Pco2 and HCO 3-, along with low arterial oxygen tension. Hypoxemia will improve with the administration of supplemental oxygen, whereas hypercapnia will persist until the resolution of ventilatory insufficiency. Pain control, incentive spirometry, and respiratory therapy with lung expansion maneuvers are key initial steps in management.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Decreased pulmonary blood flow (Choice B) may be noted in cases of pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension, right-sided heart failure, or the presence of a right-to-left shunt. Increased alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient (Choice C) occurs in cases of right-to-left shunt, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, diffusion abnormality, and dead space; the alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient is normal in cases of isolated alveolar hypoventilation. Increased metabolic demands (Choice D) generally result in increased minute ventilation. The respiratory system compensates for the increased production of carbon dioxide and organic acids through increased ventilation. Increased physiologic dead space (Choice E) may occur in cases where the alveolar membrane no longer functions correctly or is not appropriately perfused (e.g., pulmonary embolism). This results in the presence of air within an alveolus for which gas exchange does not occur. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A previously healthy 20-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his friend 1 hour after being thrown from his bicycle and striking his head on a tree . He was not wearing a helmet. He lost consciousness at the scene for less than 1 minute and then was able to stand and walk with his bicycle back to his friend's car. He fell asleep in the back seat of the car and could not be aroused when they arrived home 30 minutes later. His temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 45/min , respirations are 5/min , and blood pressure is 180/90 mm Hg. The left pupil is 6 mm and unreactive , and the right pupil is 4 mm and reactive . Examination shows intact oculocephalic and corneal reflexes . He withdraws the left upper and lower extremities to noxious stimuli but does not open his eyes or speak . The right upper extremity is flexed on the chest, and the right lower extremity is rigidly extended . CT scans of the head without contrast are shown . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: MRI of the brain with contrast

correctExplanation: Tracheal intubation and ventilation is the most appropriate next step for a patient with a decreased Glasgow Coma Scale score, bradypnea, and signs of impending central nervous system herniation. Airway management should take place prior to surgical management. In acute trauma, airway and breathing must be managed before circulation and central nervous system lesions. A patient with a compromised airway and insufficient respiratory drive is at immediate risk for decompensation. In cases of head trauma, a period of unconsciousness followed by a brief lucid interval suggests the presence of an epidural hematoma. Epidural hematomas are associated with trauma to the middle meningeal artery and result in a collection of blood dissecting the dura away from the skull. The hematoma exerts mass effect on the adjacent brain parenchyma and intracranial pressure increases. If herniation is impending, the Cushing reflex (bradycardia, hypertension, and irregular respirations) may be seen along with signs of brain stem injury including long­ tract paralysis and decorticate or decerebrate posturing. On imaging, a lenticular collection of hyperdense blood is seen between the skull and brain, bound by suture lines. Treatment includes securing the airway with intubation, controlling respirations with mechanical ventilation, and administering hypertonic saline and mannitol to decrease intracranial pressure followed by emergent neurosurgical decompression.
