questionStem: A previously healthy 20-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his friend 1 hour after being thrown from his bicycle and striking his head on a tree . He was not wearing a helmet. He lost consciousness at the scene for less than 1 minute and then was able to stand and walk with his bicycle back to his friend's car. He fell asleep in the back seat of the car and could not be aroused when they arrived home 30 minutes later. His temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 45/min , respirations are 5/min , and blood pressure is 180/90 mm Hg. The left pupil is 6 mm and unreactive , and the right pupil is 4 mm and reactive . Examination shows intact oculocephalic and corneal reflexes . He withdraws the left upper and lower extremities to noxious stimuli but does not open his eyes or speak . The right upper extremity is flexed on the chest, and the right lower extremity is rigidly extended . CT scans of the head without contrast are shown . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: MRI of the brain with contrast

correctExplanation: Tracheal intubation and ventilation is the most appropriate next step for a patient with a decreased Glasgow Coma Scale score, bradypnea, and signs of impending central nervous system herniation. Airway management should take place prior to surgical management. In acute trauma, airway and breathing must be managed before circulation and central nervous system lesions. A patient with a compromised airway and insufficient respiratory drive is at immediate risk for decompensation. In cases of head trauma, a period of unconsciousness followed by a brief lucid interval suggests the presence of an epidural hematoma. Epidural hematomas are associated with trauma to the middle meningeal artery and result in a collection of blood dissecting the dura away from the skull. The hematoma exerts mass effect on the adjacent brain parenchyma and intracranial pressure increases. If herniation is impending, the Cushing reflex (bradycardia, hypertension, and irregular respirations) may be seen along with signs of brain stem injury including long­ tract paralysis and decorticate or decerebrate posturing. On imaging, a lenticular collection of hyperdense blood is seen between the skull and brain, bound by suture lines. Treatment includes securing the airway with intubation, controlling respirations with mechanical ventilation, and administering hypertonic saline and mannitol to decrease intracranial pressure followed by emergent neurosurgical decompression.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. MRI of the brain with contrast (Choice A) is unnecessary in cases where an emergent diagnosis has been confirmed by a CT scan. MRI would offer no necessary additional information and would delay definitive emergent treatment. Intravenous corticosteroid therapy (Choice B) is indicated in cases of severe central nervous system edema (e.g., malignancy). It does not have a role in the management of acute intracranial hemorrhage. Intravenous labetalol therapy (Choice C) is contraindicated in cases of bradycardia. In the management of intracranial bleeding, maintenance of systolic blood pressure below 160 mm Hg helps prevent further accumulation of blood; however, noncardioactive medications should be chosen when bradycardia is present (e.g., nicardipine). Ventriculostomy (Choice E) is a means of relieving increased intracranial pressure through the drainage of cerebrospinal fluid via catheter placement in the lateral ventricle. This is commonly used in the treatment of hydrocephalus; however, definitive management of an epidural hematoma includes craniotomy with hematoma evacuation. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 2-day-old male newborn has a 6-hour history of shortness of breath and blue lips and extremities . He was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. He appears cyanotic . His pulse is 164/min, respirations are 68/min , and blood pressure is 60/30 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation on room air is 75% and increases to 78% with administration of 100% oxygen by face mask. Diffuse crackles are heard in both lung fields . S2 is loud; no murmur is heard. The liver edge is palpated 4 cm below the right costal margin. A chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly and moderate pulmonary congestion . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Congenital heart disease is often subdivided into cyanotic and noncyanotic types depending on the direction of blood shunting. Structural heart defects that result in flow of deoxygenated blood from the pulmonary to systemic circulations (a right-to-left shunt) classically present with cyanosis, respiratory distress, hypoxia, tachypnea, tachycardia, and hypotension generally within 1 to 7 days after birth. Common culprit lesions include truncus arteriosus, transposition of the great vessels, tricuspid atresia, tetralogy of Fallo!, and total anomalous pulmonary venous return. These lesions require the concomitant presence of a left-to-right shunt (patent ductus arteriosus) to allow for a degree of blood oxygenation. Without a left-to-right shunt, a complete absence of oxygenation can occur because of the separated circulatory systems, which is incompatible with life. In cases of a suspected congenital cyanotic heart defect, intravenous prostaglandin should be started, which maintains a patent ductus arteriosus. Administration of indomethacin or similar nonsteroidal anti­ inflammatory medications should be avoided, as these will result in closure of the ductus arteriosus. Echocardiography is required to determine the structural defects to confirm the right-to-left shunt and to assist in operative planning.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. CT scan of the chest (Choice B) can provide structural but only limited functional information about the heart, whereas an echocardiography permits analysis of structural defects, pressure, velocity, and flow of blood which is important in understanding the hemodynamics associated with structural heart disease. Administration of indomethacin (Choice C) would result in closure of the ductus arteriosus and could worsen the degree of right-to-left shunting with resultant severe hypoxia. Administration of surfactant (Choice D) may have an adjunct role in certain cases of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome because of the inadequate production of surfactant in the setting of premature birth; however, the pulmonary function in congenital heart disease is often not affected. Cardiac catheterization (Choice E) may be necessary to further assist in evaluation of the heart anatomy and intracardiac pressures, but it is not the best next step, as echocardiography is often sufficient and does not require an invasive procedure. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A previously healthy 23-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of fatigue . He reports a decrease in exercise tolerance and in overall energy during this period . He has not had chest pain or shortness of breath . He takes no medications and has no known allergies . His father and paternal uncle underwent splenectomy in their 20s; the patient is unsure of the reason for these procedures . The patient does not smoke cigarettes or use illicit drugs. He consumes two mixed drinks of gin and tonic most weekends . He appears comfortable and is not in distress . He is 180 cm (5 ft 11 in) tall and weighs 82 kg (180 lb); BMI is 25 kg/m 2• His pulse is 90/min , and blood pressure is 116/70 mm Hg. The conjunctivae are pale. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities . The spleen tip is palpated 3 cm below the left costal margin. A blood smear is shown . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Hereditary spherocytosis (HS) is a disorder of red blood cell membrane proteins that limits the ability of the cell to conform when passing through narrow capillary beds. This results in early removal of the red blood cells by the spleen and a resultant extravascular hemolysis, which causes a normocytic, hemolytic anemia. HS is the most common disorder of the red blood cell membrane. Positive family history is generally present. Patients typically present with fatigue, weakness, and pallor, with associated splenomegaly and jaundice on physical examination. Laboratory evaluation generally discloses anemia and an indirect hyperbilirubinemia along with an abnormal osmotic fragility test and eosin-5'-maleimide analysis on flow cytometry. Blood smear demonstrates rounded red blood cells without central pallor. Splenic congestion and sequestration are hallmarks of moderate to severe disease. Splenectomy is indicated to reduce the degree of premature red blood cell consumption (extravascular hemolysis) and the risk for sequestration crises.
incorrectExplanation: nd G. Avoidance of fava beans {Choice A) is appropriate in patients with glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, as red blood cell hemolysis can ensue in the setting of oxidative stressors. Genetic testing {Choice B) is appropriate in assessing the patient's risk for transmitting HS to offspring, but identifying a specific mutation is neither required to confirm HS nor to guide therapy. Hydroxyurea therapy {Choice C) inhibits ribonucleotide reductase. It is used primarily in the treatment of sickle cell disease, as it increases the production of fetal hemoglobin, a substitute for dysfunctional hemoglobin. Iron supplementation {Choice D) is appropriate in the treatment of microcytic iron-deficiency anemia. HS is a defect in red blood cell structure, not in the metabolism of iron. Prednisone therapy {Choice E) is used in many inflammatory, infectious, and neoplastic disease states. It does not have a recognized role in the management of HS. Vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin) supplementation {Choice F) is appropriate for use in macrocytic anemia with megaloblastosis arising from Vitamin B 12 (cobalamin) deficiency (e.g., veganism, pernicious anemia, Crohn disease). It does not have a recognized role in the management of HS. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 77-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being rescued from a house fire. Firefighters found him unconscious in his bed; the bedroom was full of smoke . The firefighters and paramedics state that the patient probably fell asleep while smoking in bed. On arrival , he does not respond to verbal stimuli and has cough productive of carbonaceous sputum . His temperature is 37.8°C (100°F) , pulse is 120/min, respirations are 30/min and labored , and blood pressure is 98/78 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on 50% oxygen by face mask shows an oxygen saturation of 93%. Examination shows second degree burns over the face and upper extremities . There is marked facial edema , and the eyebrows are singed. On pulmonary examination , air movement is poor. Stridor and wheezes are heard over the lung bases bilaterally. The patient's carboxyhemoglobin concentration is 35%. Arterial blood gas analysis on 50% oxygen by face mask shows : pH 7.25 Pco2 65 mm Hg Po2 45 mm Hg After endotracheal intubation and administration of 100% oxygen, this patient should receive fluid resuscitation with which of the following during the next 12 hours?
correctExplanation: Partial-thickness (second-degree), full-thickness (third-degree), or fourth-degree burns (extension to muscle, bone, and/or joints) compromise the ability of the skin to maintain fluid balance. Exposure to a hot environment such as a fire can result in large insensible evaporative fluid losses to the external environment because of compromise of the epidermal barrier, while the cutaneous burns themselves result in third­ spacing and intravascular losses to dermal edema. These losses are further exacerbated by tachypnea or airway burns resulting in additional insensible losses and pulmonary edema, respectively. Fluid resuscitation in second, third, and fourth-degree burns is achieved through administration of isotonic crystalloid solution, which is the standard of care. The amount is guided by the Parkland formula, which calculates the amount of fluid to administer over the first day based on the percentage of body surface area burned (second, third, and fourth-degree burns only) and the weight of the patient. Resuscitation should be additionally guided based on clinical parameters including hemodynamic stability, glomerular filtration rate, electrolyte disturbances, and urine output.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Colloid and isotonic crystalloid solution (Choice A) is incorrect as colloids are generally not deficient in the setting of burns (e.g., albumin). The administration of isotonic crystalloids alone is the standard of care for resuscitative fluid administration as it provides the most direct intravascular benefit. Fresh frozen plasma (Choice B) is appropriate for use as a resuscitation fluid in cases of severe blood loss as part of a balanced resuscitation treatment plan. It is also used in reversing anticoagulation when prothrombin complex concentrates are not available. It does not have a primary role in the fluid resuscitation of patients with burns. Hypertonic crystalloid solution only (Choice C) is used in the management of acute hyponatremia with neurologic deficits and to reduce cerebral edema in cases of elevated intracranial pressure. It does not have a primary role in the fluid resuscitation of patients with burns. Packed red blood cells (Choice E) are used as a component of resuscitation in cases of hemorrhagic shock. Unless blood loss or severe anemia is also present, they are not used in the fluid resuscitation of patients with burns. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: An 8-year-old girl has had migrating polyarthralgia and fever for 4 days. She appears ill. Examination shows an evanescent rash. Her left knee is red, swollen , and tender. The chest is clear to auscultation . A grade 4/6, holosystolic apical murmur is heard with radiation to the axilla . There is no organomegaly . Which of the following is the most likely cardiac abnormality?
correctExplanation: Acute rheumatic fever (ARF) may present with migratory polyarthralgia, pancarditis (pericarditis, myocarditis, or endocarditis), subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, Sydenham chorea, fever, increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and short PR interval following an infection from group A streptococci, most often pharyngitis. The mitral valve is the most commonly affected. Antibodies to M protein enhance host defenses against group A streptococci but can result in an autoimmune attack against self-antigens through molecular mimicry. This can result in valve inflammation and acute regurgitation. Chronic mitral regurgitation, prolapse, or stenosis can result as potential long-term sequelae.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Aortic stenosis (Choice A) presents with a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur that is heard best at the upper right sternal border and radiates to the carotid arteries. It classically occurs secondary to age-related fibrotic and calcific changes of the valve but can occur earlier in life in cases of bicuspid aortic valve or chronic rheumatic disease. Tetralogy of Fallo! (Choice C) consists of pulmonary infundibular stenosis, overriding aorta, ventricular septal defect, and right ventricular hypertrophy, resulting in a right-to-left shunt with cyanosis first noted in infancy. The murmur heard with Tetralogy of Fallo! relates to the underlying ventricular septal defect, characterized by a holosystolic murmur heard best in the lower left sternal border, and to the pulmonic stenosis, characterized by a systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur in the pulmonic listening area. Tricuspid regurgitation (Choice D) demonstrates a holosystolic murmur heard best in the lower left sternal border. The tricuspid valve is less commonly affected than the mitral or aortic valves in ARF. Ventricular septal defect (VSD) (Choice E) is characterized by a holosystolic murmur heard best in the lower left sternal border. VSD generally presents at birth and is not associated with ARF. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 24-year-old man comes to the emergency department 60 minutes after the sudden onset of tearing chest pain radiating to his back. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications . He does not smoke. He is 190 cm (6 ft 3 in) tall and weighs 80 kg (176 lb); BMI is 22 kg/m2• His temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg in his right arm and 70/40 mm Hg in his left arm. Pulse oximetry on 2 L/min of oxygen via nasal cannula shows an oxygen saturation of 100%. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities . The lungs are clear to auscultation . Heart sounds are normal. Pulses are difficult to palpate in the left upper extremity. Peripheral pulses are otherwise normal. A chest x-ray shows a widened upper mediastinum . An ECG shows sinus tachycardia with no acute changes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Labetalol is a first-line antihypertensive medication used to decrease blood pressure in the setting of presumed aortic dissection, which classically presents with severe, acute, tearing chest pain radiating to the back, differential blood pressures between extremities, and a widened mediastinum on a chest x-ray. To prevent further progression of the dissection flap, controlling the patient's heart rate and blood pressure is the first priority. An intravenous ~-adrenergic blocking agent should be used with a goal of decreasing the heart rate to approximately 60/min and the blood pressure to less than 100 to 120 mm Hg systolic and 60 to 80 mm Hg diastolic. Decreasing the heart rate helps prevent the advancement of the dissection flap and resultant occlusion of branch vessels by limiting the pulse pressure differential. Labetalol is a nonspecific adrenoreceptor blocker that targets both ar and ~radrenoreceptors, making it an ideal choice for the management of the patient's heart rate, cardiac contractility, and vascular resistance.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Administration of heparin (Choice A) would be appropriate in the management of an acute coronary syndrome. Administering therapeutic anticoagulation in the setting of an aortic dissection increases the risk for severe thoracic hemorrhage and exsanguination if there is an associated aneurysm and/or damage to the tunica adventitia. Administration of nitroglycerin (Choice C) may be appropriate in cases of aortic dissection for blood pressure control if the goal is not met with adrenoreceptor blockade; however, it would follow administration of a ~­ adrenergic blocking agent to prevent reflex tachycardia and widening of pulse pressure. Fiberoptic intubation (Choice D) may be appropriate for a patient with a compromised airway, but in cases without an impending threat to the airway would be superseded by management of the immediate life­ threatening condition, the patient's aortic dissection. Pericardiocentesis (Choice E) is appropriate in cases of pericardia! effusion and/or tamponade, which would present following symptoms of pericarditis, or with muffled heart sounds, jugular venous distention, and hypotension iftamponade from any cause is present. Pulsus paradoxus may be seen on examination. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 62-year-old woman comes to the physician because of ulcers on her right ankle for 6 months . There is no history of recent trauma . She has a 5-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with insulin for the past 4 years and a 2-year history of chronic bilateral ankle swelling . Her temperature is 37.?°C (99.9°F), pulse is 82/min , and blood pressure is 140/88 mm Hg. Examination shows ulceration of the medial aspect of the right ankle. There is bilateral lower leg and pedal edema with patches of brown pigmentation . Peripheral pulses are present and normal. Which of the following is the most likely pathogenesis of this condition?
correctExplanation: Venous insufficiency presents with dependent, pitting edema that improves with compression and elevation, along with paresthesia and hyperpigmentation of the skin (e.g., stasis dermatitis). In severe cases, chronic circulatory insufficiency can result in skin breakdown, leading to the development of open ulcers, classically along the medial aspect of the ankle. Venous insufficiency often results from deep venous thrombosis with resultant damage to the valves. When the thrombus resolves, the residual vessel may be dysfunctional from damage to the valve leaflets, valve annulus, or increased diameter of the native vessel. This prevents the vessel from functioning effectively and results in stagnant or retrograde venous flow secondary to gravity. Treatment includes wound care for the ulcer and measures to reverse the venous insufficiency such as optimizing venous return, diuresis, and improving circulatory function by optimizing cardiac, vascular, and kidney function.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Arterial insufficiency {Choice A) classically presents with claudication; thin, waxy, hairless skin; an absence of edema; and painful ulcers classically along the outer ankle, foot, or distal toes. Congestive heart failure {Choice B) presents with shortness of breath, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, peripheral edema, jugular venous distention, crackles on examination, and an S3 or S4 gallop. It may be an indirect cause of venous congestion through stasis and hypervolemia. Neurotrophic ulcer {Choice C) results from repetitive trauma or compression in areas of impaired sensation. Such ulcers are commonly seen overlying bony prominences (e.g., metatarsal heads) in cases of peripheral neuropathy from diabetes mellitus. Thromboangiitis obliterans {Choice D) is also known as Buerger disease and is a small vessel vasculitis associated with smoking. It typically presents with claudication symptoms that may progress to ulceration, gangrene, and autoamputation of digits. Ulcerations tend to occur in the tips of the fingers and toes. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 42-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of generalized itching and fatigue . He has chronic renal failure secondary to glomerulonephritis and receives hemodialysis three times weekly. Examination shows no abnormalities except for a patent arteriovenous fistula in the left forearm . His serum calcium concentration is 8.3 mg/dl , serum phosphorus concentration is 4.1 mg/dl , and serum intact parathyroid hormone concentration is 485 pg/ml (N=10-65) . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Secondary hyperparathyroidism typically presents with increased parathyroid hormone (PTH), hypocalcemia, and hyperphosphatemia. It results from end-stage kidney disease because of the inability of the kidney to excrete phosphate and to produce active vitamin D, which results in hypocalcemia. Hyperphosphatemia and hypocalcemia result in the upregulation of PTH, which increases bony turnover to raise serum calcium and promotes renal excretion of phosphate. When unregulated, this process results in renal osteodystrophy which is the breakdown of bone because of excessive PTH stimulus of osteoclasts.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Familial hypercalcemic hypocalciuria {Choice A) arises from an abnormal calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid cells. As a result, PTH is not suppressed by normal or increased serum calcium. This leads to mild hypercalcemia with increased PTH because of the normal mechanism of action of PTH on osteoclasts and renal tubules. Cinacalcet is used to treat the condition, which increases the sensitivity of the calcium-sensing receptor to the presence of serum calcium. Paraneoplastic syndrome {Choice B) defines a pathologic state that arises secondary to the presence of a malignancy; for example, squamous cell carcinoma of the lung may exogenously produce PTH-related peptide (PTH-rP) which functions in the same manner as PTH. Endogenous PTH is downregulated in the setting of exogenous PTH-rP. Primary hyperparathyroidism {Choice C) presents with hypercalcemia, hypophosphatemia, and increased PTH. It occurs because of a parathyroid adenoma, hyperplasia, or carcinoma. Tertiary hyperparathyroidism {Choice E) describes a state of chronic, refractory, autonomous production of PTH in the setting of long-standing kidney disease and presents with hypercalcemia, normal or increased serum phosphate, and increased PTH. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A previously healthy 15-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after the sudden onset of difficulty breathing and sharp chest pain that began during track practice . She is 183 cm (6 ft) tall and weighs 55 kg (121 lb); BMI is 16 kg/m2. On arrival , her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F) , pulse is 70/min , and respirations are 28/min . Breath sounds are decreased over the lateral chest on the right; there is hyperresonance to percussion . Cardiac examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of these findings?

choices.A: Air collection in the pleural space

correctExplanation: Pneumothorax results from air entering the intrapleural space from either an external (e.g., stab wound) or internal (e.g., ruptured bleb or bronchus, bronchopleural fistula) source. As the air accumulates within the space, the lung parenchyma becomes compressed, resulting in respiratory distress, reduced breath sounds, hyperresonance to percussion, and in severe cases, tension on the mediastinal structures impeding venous return resulting in hypotension. A spontaneous primary pneumothorax can occur in a tall, thin, young person because of the rupture of a pulmonary bleb, classically in a young athlete and often during physical exertion. Small pneumothoraces can be managed with serial examinations and repeat chest x-rays to confirm resolution. When the lesion is larger than 20 to 30% of the hemithoracic volume, a chest tube should be placed to evacuate the pneumothorax and reinflate the lung to prevent the development of a persistent or permanent pneumothorax. Tension pneumothorax should be immediately decompressed with emergent needle thoracostomy to prevent hemodynamic collapse.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Alveolar atelectasis (Choice B) may present with shortness of breath or be asymptomatic depending on the size and extent. A small, subsegmental atelectatic region may be completely asymptomatic, whereas if an entire lung is involved, the patient may present with shortness of breath, severe hypoxia, diminished ipsilateral breath sounds, and dullness to percussion. Narrowing of moderate-sized airways (Choice C) presents with poor air movement, wheezing or rhonchi, and cough, and describes the pathophysiology of bronchitis. Asthma classically results in narrowing of the small airways. Pleural inflammation (Choice D) presents with pleuritic chest pain, often following a viral respiratory infection. Occasionally, a friction rub may be heard on auscultation, but often the examination and vital signs are unremarkable. Pulmonary parenchymal inflammation (Choice E) describes pneumonitis or pneumonia, which typically presents with chest pain, shortness of breath, and cough; hyperresonance to percussion would not be expected. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 77-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital because of severe cramping pain in the lower abdomen . The pain has been constant for the past 16 hours. The abdomen is markedly distended . A McBurney incisional scar is noted in the right lower quadrant. The x-ray shown was taken shortly after admission . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.C: Mechanical obstruction of the small intestine

correctExplanation: A sigmoid volvulus results from twisting of the sigmoid mesentery, which can lead to large bowel obstruction and perforation or intestinal necrosis if not treated. Patients commonly present with symptoms secondary to a large bowel obstruction such as constipation, abdominal bloating, distention, nausea, and vomiting. Sigmoid volvulus typically demonstrates a coffee-bean appearance on abdominal x-rays with severe distention of the sigmoid colon. In patients without complications such as bowel ischemia or perforation, treatment requires detorsion of the sigmoid colon and mesentery through sigmoidoscopy with placement of a rectal tube to facilitate stool passage and maintain decompression. Recurrent sigmoid volvulus may require surgical colopexy or sigmoid colectomy.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Cecal cancer (Choice A) is often asymptomatic until late in the course. It is classically associated with occult gastrointestinal bleeding and iron deficiency anemia. lleoileal intussusception (Choice B) describes telescoping of one segment of ileum into an adjacent segment, which can cause intestinal ischemia or obstruction. It typically occurs because of a pathologic lead point (e.g., malignancy, stricture, lymphadenopathy), and presents with colicky pain and bloating. Abdominal x-rays are often nondiagnostic for the condition, which is better detailed on ultrasonography (children) or CT scan (adults), which will disclose the intussusceptum. Mechanical obstruction of the small intestine (Choice C) is typically acute, occurring because of adhesions, inflammatory bowel disease, strictures, malignancies, or hernias. It typically presents with abdominal pain, nausea, nonbloody and sometimes bilious emesis, hyperactive and high-pitched bowel sounds, and abdominal distention. X-rays may show dilated loops of small bowel with air-fluid levels. Paralytic ileus (Choice D) refers to intestinal hypomotility without a mechanical obstruction, most commonly occurring following surgery or in the setting of electrolyte abnormalities (e.g., end-stage kidney disease resulting in hyperkalemia). It typically presents with diffuse small and large bowel dilatation. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the emergency department 24 hours after the onset of severe abdominal cramps and nausea . During this period , she has vomited yellow-green material once and has had only two bowel movements , which were small and liquid. During the past 6 months , she has had less severe abdominal cramps associated with diarrhea and a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight loss. She says the cramps have become more severe during the past month. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications . On arrival , she is in moderate distress . She appears pale. She is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall and weighs 52 kg (114 lb); BMI is 19 kg/m 2. Her temperature is 37 .2°C (99°F), pulse is 90/min , and blood pressure is 116/78 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows moderate distention with mild right lower quadrant tenderness . Her leukocyte count is 14,000/mm 3• A CT scan of the abdomen shows thickening of the terminal ileum and air in the rectum. The colon is not dilated. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.B: Upper gastrointestinal series with a water-soluble contrast and small bowel follow-through

correctExplanation: Crohn disease is characterized by transmural inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract, most frequently involving the terminal ileum. It can arise anywhere in the gastrointestinal tract and is a subclass of inflammatory bowel disease. Most patients experience chronic abdominal cramping, bloody diarrhea, anemia, and weight loss. Examination often demonstrates generalized abdominal tenderness, sometimes worse in the right lower quadrant, and, depending on the severity and extent, may disclose complications such as enterocutaneous fistulas and extraintestinal manifestations such as uveitis. Severe Crohn disease can result in intestinal obstruction from stricture or inflammation, bowel perforation, intra-abdominal abscess, and the formation of additional fistulas. Diagnosis occurs through colonoscopy with biopsy, which is the best next step in the diagnosis of this patient. Laboratory analyses often disclose increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein concentration. Treatment is through anti-inflammatory medications, immunomodulators, and glucocorticoids, with complicated, severe cases sometimes requiring surgery including small bowel resection or colectomy.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Barium enema (Choice A) is used to evaluate the lumen of the large bowel to assist in the diagnosis of colonic neoplasms, strictures, fistulas, or postsurgical complications. It does not reliably image the distal small bowel and does not permit sampling of tissue for biopsy. Upper gastrointestinal series with a water-soluble contrast and small bowel follow-through (Choice B) studies are indicated when structural lesions involving the stomach or small bowel are suspected. This is most commonly indicated for the evaluation of small bowel pathology, such as duodenal atresia, malrotation with volvulus, and Crohn disease; however, it would not offer the opportunity to sample tissue through biopsy. MRI of the abdomen (Choice C) offers high-contrast resolution detail of soft-tissue structures within the abdomen. It can be used for the evaluation of a variety of intra-abdominal pathologies. MRI enterography techniques can be utilized to investigate sites of active or chronic bowel inflammation, although this would not permit tissue sampling. Capsule endoscopy (Choice D) is used in the diagnosis of jejunal and proximal ileal pathology located outside of the reachable field of view of upper endoscopy or colonoscopy. It is most commonly used in the workup of small bowel sources of gastrointestinal bleeding or neoplasia. It offers images only and cannot be used for tissue sampling. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A previously healthy 32-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after a motor vehicle collision . She was an unrestrained front seat passenger . On arrival, she has pain and tingling in her right leg and is unable to move it. Her pulse is 105/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 155/90 mm Hg. The right lower extremity is pale. The dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are absent on the right. There is a posterior dislocation of the right knee. Motor and sensory function is absent below the right knee. Following reduction of the dislocation and splinting of the right lower extremity, the patient is able to move the leg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.A: Venous duplex ultrasonography of the right lower extremity
choices.B: CT scan of the right lower extremity

correctExplanation: Posterior knee dislocation places traction on the popliteal artery and branches of the sciatic nerve. Such an injury can result in potential circulatory insufficiency and neurological deficits to the leg distal to the level of the injury, resulting in permanent loss of function if untreated. Prompt reduction of the knee dislocation serves to limit the extent of injury by relieving neurovascular traction, thereby minimizing damage and restoring nerve function and arterial flow. Arterial injuries sustained during a posterior knee dislocation can include dissection, rupture, thrombosis, and intramural hematoma; pseudoaneurysms can also occur. Prompt arteriography or CT/MR angiography is indicated to further investigate the presence of underlying arterial injuries and to facilitate operative repair planning.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Venous duplex ultrasonography of the right lower extremity (Choice A) is appropriate to investigate the diagnosis of deep venous thrombosis, which can result from stasis in the setting of orthopaedic injury. However, it is not the most likely immediate complication of a knee dislocation. CT scan of the right lower extremity (Choice B) provides detail about bony, vascular, and soft tissue structures; however, a CT angiography protocol would be required for appropriate vessel imaging detail. Arthroscopy (Choice C) may eventually be required in the diagnosis or repair of potentially damaged knee ligaments from the dislocation; however, this is not the most immediate limb-threatening complication. Nerve conduction studies (Choice E) may eventually be indicated to diagnose injury to the distal sciatic nerve branches such as the tibial and peroneal nerves but would not take precedence over arterial injury assessment in a patient where motor function had been restored. No further diagnostic studies necessary (Choice F) is inappropriate; posterior knee dislocation is highly associated with arterial injury and additional studies are indicated to prevent a delay in diagnosis and treatment. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 70-year-old man has a 2-year history of progressive dysphagia and intermittent regurgitation of undigested food . A barium swallow is shown . Which of the following is the most likely cause?
correctExplanation: A pharyngoesophageal (Zenker) diverticulum occurs within the hypopharynx, just above or at the level of the cricopharyngeus muscle. The mechanism of formation includes an uncoordinated swallowing mechanism, which results in muscle spasms of the cricopharyngeus leading to pulsion diverticula as the wall of the hypopharynx and superior esophagus weakens. Symptoms include halitosis, regurgitation of undigested food, and dysphagia. Barium swallow discloses a posterior, midline outpouching above or at the level of the cricopharyngeus. Treatment includes surgical repair and resection (diverticulectomy), plus dietary modifications to include soft or liquid foods.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Absence of peristalsis after swallowing (Choice A) occurs in the setting of autonomic neuropathy, cerebrovascular accident, and achalasia. It generally results in the failure of a food bolus to transit through the hypopharynx and/or esophagus, not in the focal formation of a hypopharyngeal diverticulum. Diffuse esophageal spasm (Choice C) presents with severe dysphagia and chest pain, often acutely in the setting of swallowing. It may also occur in the absence of swallowing, such as in association with gastroesophageal reflux disease. Barium swallow would disclose a "corkscrew" esophagus, not a focal hypopharyngeal diverticulum. Severe gastroesophageal reflux (Choice D) presents with cough, sour or metallic taste, chest discomfort, and nausea. It is often worse when supine or following the ingestion of trigger foods. It would not be expected to cause a focal hypopharyngeal diverticulum. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 37-year-old woman is scheduled for operative treatment of an umbilical hernia with incarcerated omentum under general anesthesia . During the operation , a solid nodule is excised , and a frozen section shows metastatic carcinoma consistent with primary ovarian cancer. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

choices.A: Close the operative site and discuss further treatment with the patient when she awakens
choices.B: Place a central venous catheter with a subcutaneous injection port for chemotherapy and discuss further treatment with the patient when she awakens
choices.C: Place a peritoneal dialysis catheter through the operative site for future chemotherapy and discuss further treatment with the patient when she awakens
choices.D: Obtain consent from the next of kin and place a central venous catheter with a subcutaneous injection port for chemotherapy
choices.E: Obtain consent from the next of kin and proceed with laparotomy and tumor debulking

correctExplanation: Incidental discoveries during unrelated surgery, when not immediately life-threatening, are appropriately managed by closing the operative site and discussing the findings with the patient when they regain decision­ making capacity following anesthesia. While discovery of malignancy in a young woman may immediately prompt the thought that treatment would be desired, the decision to pursue intervention is ultimately the patient's choice, upholding the ethical principle of autonomy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Placing a central venous catheter with a subcutaneous injection port for chemotherapy and discussing further treatment with the patient when she awakens (Choice B) and placing a peritoneal dialysis catheter through the operative site for future chemotherapy and discussing further treatment with the patient when she awakens (Choice C) do not respect the patient's autonomy and do not consider her preferences in treatment. Obtain consent from the next of kin and place a central venous catheter with a subcutaneous injection port for chemotherapy (Choice D) and obtaining consent from the next of kin and proceeding with laparotomy and tumor debulking (Choice E) are also incorrect. These choices violate the patient's autonomy, and there is no suspicion of a lack of decision-making capacity outside of the time the patient is under anesthesia. In cases where the patient would not be able to make a decision because of an absence of capacity, a surrogate decision maker can be used. However, unless a procedure is urgent or emergent, there is no immediate need to consult a surrogate. The patient can recover capacity from the anesthesia with a decision made after further discussions. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: An 82-year-old woman is brought to the physician for a follow-up examination 2 months after she sustained a right hip fracture when she fell in her kitchen . Two years ago, she sustained a Colles fracture in a fall. Examination today shows a well-healed scar over the right hip. Range of motion of the hip joint is full. Her serum calcium concentration is within the reference ranges ; her serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentration is decreased . A DEXA scan shows osteoporosis . Which of the following is the most likely additional serum abnormality in this patient?
correctExplanation: Osteoporosis occurs because of the loss of bone mineral density. The condition results from the interplay of three possible mechanisms: failure to achieve peak bone density, increased bone resorption, and decreased new bone formation. The condition is often asymptomatic until a traumatic injury results in a fracture, most commonly involving the hip, distal radius, or vertebrae. Classically, serum calcium, vitamin D, and magnesium concentrations are within the reference ranges; however, calcium handling in the bloodstream is key in the pathogenesis of osteoporosis. Hypocalcemia and hypovitaminosis D both lead to increased concentrations of parathyroid hormone (PTH), which results in increased osteoclast activity and bone resorption. Low concentrations of vitamin D are also associated with increased concentrations of PTH even when serum calcium is within the reference range. The diagnosis of osteoporosis is made based on DEXA scan once the bone density falls below 2.5 standard deviations of the mean for a young adult. Treatment includes correcting any modifiable risk factors, supplementing calcium and vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise therapy, and the use of osteoclast inhibitors (e.g., bisphosphonates).
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Decreased 1 a-hydroxylase activity (Choice A) results in a low active vitamin D concentration in the setting of end-stage kidney disease because of loss of parenchymal cells that synthesize the enzyme and the resultant inability to convert 25-hydroxyvitamin D to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, the active form. A deficiency of this enzyme would be uncommon outside of a primary kidney disease. Nutritional deficiency of vitamin D is more likely when the precursor 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentration is low. Decreased thyroxine (T 4) concentration (Choice B) presents with symptoms of hypothyroidism including weight gain, lethargy, fatigue, constipation, hair loss, and cold intolerance. Thyroid hormone promotes bone mineral density; however, in the absence of additional symptoms of hypothyroidism, a deficiency of thyroxine is less likely. Increased calcitonin concentration (Choice C) classically presents with hypocalcemia, as calcitonin promotes osteoblast activity with resultant bone mineral deposition. Increased osteocalcin concentration (Choice D) is a marker of bone formation and is correlated with increases in bone mineral density, for example, when bone-forming medications such as teriparatide are used. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 25-year-old man comes for a routine health maintenance examination. A harsh systolic murmur is heard. Examination shows no other abnormalities . Echocardiography shows a bicuspid aortic valve . This patient is at increased risk for aortic stenosis as a result of which of the following?
correctExplanation: Calcification of the valve is a pathologic consequence of mechanical stresses on heart valves and results from repetitive microtrauma from the opening and closing of valve leaflets with associated chronic inflammation. Many people will develop some degree of valve stenosis because of chronic inflammation with resultant calcification and fibrosis over time, with the aortic valve most commonly affected. Structural abnormalities of the valve, such as a bicuspid aortic valve, alter the biomechanics of valve opening and closing, which increases the likelihood of earlier calcification and resultant stenosis because of increased mechanical trauma. Congenital bicuspid aortic valve classically presents with early signs and symptoms of aortic stenosis and left-sided diastolic heart failure. Patients may report fatigue, shortness of breath, cough, diminished exercise tolerance, or syncope with exertion. Examination findings include a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur heard best at the upper right sternal border, and pulsus parvus et tardus (weak and delayed) may be noted on examination of peripheral pulses. Because of the chronic increased afterload from a fixed obstruction by the valve, left ventricular hypertrophy and resultant diastolic dysfunction can occur. If early aortic stenosis occurs, the patient may be a candidate for aortic valve replacement.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Formation of atherosclerotic plaque (Choice B) describes the principal risk factor for coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular accidents, and peripheral artery disease. The presence of a plaque within the arterial wall acts as a nidus for thrombus formation when the plaque ruptures. This does not play a role in the development of aortic stenosis. Rupture of the chordae tendineae (Choice C) may occur following a myocardial infarction. It typically leads to acute valvular regurgitation and is classically associated with acute pulmonary edema from mitral regurgitation. Streptococcal infection (Choice D) is associated with rheumatic heart disease, which results in inflammation of the valves of the heart, most commonly the mitral and aortic valves. This may present with acute regurgitant murmurs and chronically can result in stenosis. This patient's bicuspid aortic valve is his main risk factor for early-onset aortic stenosis. Thrombus deposition on the valve (Choice E) is commonly seen in cases of mechanical valve replacement with subtherapeutic anticoagulation. The nonendothelialized valve surface acts as a nidus for thrombus formation. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: An 18-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 20 minutes after she sustained severe head injuries in a high-speed motor vehicle collision in which she was the unrestrained driver. Paramedics report finding a bottle of amphetamines inside the patient's vehicle . On arrival , her Glasgow Coma Scale score is 6, and she is immediately intubated . Her pulse is 50/min , and blood pressure is 180/90 mm Hg. Examination shows numerous ecchymoses ; lacerations over the face , trunk , and upper extremities ; and right-sided hemotympanum . There are obvious facial fractures . Except for an abrasion over the right upper quadrant , abdominal examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's increased blood pressure?

choices.F: Pain response related to the fractures

correctExplanation: The Cushing reflex presents with systemic hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respirations. It is observed during periods of increased intracranial pressure, often in the setting of impending herniation. As intracranial pressure rises, often because of intracranial bleeding (e.g., traumatic epidural or subdural hematoma) and/or cerebral edema, mean arterial pressure rises to maintain cerebral perfusion pressure. In response to rising mean arterial pressure, carotid baroreceptors trigger reflex bradycardia as an autoregulatory response. Irregular respirations occur because of compression of the pons and medulla, which control autonomic respiratory rate and pattern. The presence of the Cushing reflex suggests increased intracranial pressure in extremis and constitutes a neurosurgical emergency. Immediate treatment to decrease intracranial pressure is required, including administration of mannitol, hypertonic saline, hyperventilation, and elevation of the head of the bed with emergent decompressive surgery.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Acute renal artery dissection (Choice A) can cause secondary hypertension from activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, though clinical evidence including thoracoabdominal trauma, flank bruising, or a bruit may be present. Bradycardia and head trauma with signs of a basilar skull fracture (hemotympanum) are more suggestive of intracranial bleeding. Amphetamine intoxication (Choice B) and increased serum catecholamine concentration (Choice E) present with signs of sympathomimetic toxicity including hypertension, tachycardia, tachypnea, diaphoresis, and dilated pupils. Decreased minute ventilation (Choice C) does not generally have a direct causal relationship with mean arterial pressure; however, it can be associated with increased intracranial pressure through respiratory acidosis inducing cerebral vasodilation. Pain response related to the fractures (Choice F) is variably associated with signs of sympathetic or parasympathetic stimulus, which would include hypertension and tachycardia in the setting of increased sympathetic stimulus, or bradycardia and hypotension in the event of a vagal response to pain. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 55-year-old man comes to the physician's office because of claudication . He smokes two packs of cigarettes per day and has no history of diabetes mellitus . The femoral pulses are palpable bilaterally, and distal pulses are absent. Capillary refill in both feet is less than 5 seconds . Ankle-arm indices are 0.75 on the right and 0.60 on the left. In addition to recommending that he quit smoking , which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in patient care?
correctExplanation: Prescription for an exercise program is the most appropriate initial step in management for this patient. Leg pain that occurs following exertion and improves with rest is known as claudication and indicates the presence of peripheral vascular disease. Claudication results from increased physiologic demand of the skeletal musculature for oxygen, which cannot be met because of the fixed obstruction to flow of stenotic arteries. As demand falls during rest, the pain typically improves. Peripheral vascular disease is common among older men who smoke cigarettes and have a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, or hyperlipidemia. Active exercise improves collateral vascularization, which allows for improved arterial oxygenated blood flow to the skeletal musculature and is the best initial step in treatment along with the mitigation of risk factors. Additional therapeutic options include cilostazol and surgical revascularization (e.g., bypass, stenting), which can be employed following exercise therapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Balloon angioplasty (Choice A) and femoropopliteal bypass (Choice B) are both invasive options that should be reserved for when noninvasive therapy is no longer sufficient. Sympathectomy (Choice C) refers to the removal of a sympathetic nerve root and is often used in hyperhidrosis, reflex sympathetic dystrophy, and Raynaud disease. The disease cause of claudication is generally not because of sympathetically mediated vasoconstriction, and sympathectomy does not generally play a role in treatment. Vasodilator therapy (Choice D) (e.g., cilostazol) may have a role in treating this patient's claudication, but it will not promote collateral vascularization which improves long-term symptoms. Because of this, initial treatment with a regimented exercise program is recommended. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 57-year-old woman is undergoing elective endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with 20% benzocaine spray for analgesia and intravenous meperidine and midazolam for sedation . She is receiving 100% oxygen (5 L/min) by nasal cannula . Ten minutes after initiation of the procedure , she becomes mildly confused and cyanotic . She does not have chest or abdominal pain. She has a 5-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus controlled with metformin . She had a myocardial infarction and coronary artery bypass grafting 3 years ago and has not had cardiac symptoms since then . Laparoscopic cholecystectomy was performed 1 year ago; abdominal ultrasonography 2 weeks ago showed a dilated common bile duct with retained calculi. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years . Her pulse is 106/min, respirations are 30/min , and blood pressure is 116/78 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry shows a decrease in oxygen saturation from 99% to 84% during the past 10 minutes ; oxygen saturation improves significantly with 40% oxygen by face mask. A few crackles are heard at the lung bases. Laboratory studies show: Arterial blood gas analysis shows : Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Administration of 100% oxygen by nonrebreather face mask

correctExplanation: Hemoglobin Methemoglobin Carboxyhemoglobin Pco2 Po2 0 2 saturation 41% (N:51 .5) 2% (N:55) 43 mm Hg 282 mm Hg 99% Methemoglobinemia occurs when an abnormal fraction of hemoglobin in the blood exists in the ferric (Fe 3•) form (methemoglobin). Methemoglobin cannot effectively bind oxygen, which impairs tissue oxygen delivery. Most cases of methemoglobinemia are acquired, typically because of exposure to an oxidant stressor such as an anesthetic (e.g., benzocaine), nitrate, or dapsone. Symptoms include shortness of breath, fatigue, lethargy, light-headedness, and in severe cases, arrhythmia, seizure, and multisystem organ failure. Vital signs typically demonstrate reduced oxygen saturation, and examination may show cyanosis. Characteristically, blood appears darkened ("chocolate-colored blood") on gross visualization. Treatment includes supplemental oxygen plus intravenous administration of methylene blue, a reducing agent that donates electrons to heme. Reduction to the ferrous (Fe 2•) form restores the ability of hemoglobin to bind, carry, and deliver oxygen to tissues.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Administration of 100% oxygen by nonrebreather face mask (Choice A) is an acceptable strategy for supplemental oxygenation in cases of methemoglobinemia; however, this patient is already receiving oxygen by face mask, and the arterial blood gas analysis demonstrates appropriate partial pressure of oxygen in the bloodstream. Additional supplemental oxygen would have no further clinical benefit to the patient. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (Choice B) is appropriate in cases of carbon monoxide poisoning leading to hypoxia and end-organ damage. Methemoglobinemia results from oxidation of heme, not from competitive binding by carbon monoxide. Reduction of heme and improved transport of oxygen would not be achieved through hyperbaric therapy. Exchange transfusion (Choice C) can theoretically replace dysfunctional methemoglobin; however, the inciting factor may still be present within the patient, which could further convert replaced hemoglobin to methemoglobin, nullifying the value in any transfusion. Methylene blue is a safer and more effective treatment for methemoglobinemia. Mechanical ventilation (Choice E) is indicated in cases of hypoxemic or hypercapnic respiratory failure not responsive to noninvasive therapies. It is not appropriate in a patient who is awake and demonstrates intact r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 62-year-old man with alcoholism comes to the emergency department because he has vomited bright red blood three times during the past 6 hours. His pulse is 130/min, and blood pressure is 90/40 mm Hg. He becomes dizzy when he sits up. Abdominal examination shows marked distention, shifting dullness , and a fluid wave . Upper endoscopy shows esophageal varices and an ulcer with a blood clot on a visible vessel located on the posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.C: Intravenous fluid therapy and blood transfusion
choices.D: Endoscopic-guided sclerosis of the esophageal varices
choices.E: Placement of a transjugular intrahepatic portal shunt

correctExplanation: Tachycardia and hypotension in the setting of gastrointestinal bleeding is diagnostic of decompensated hemorrhagic shock, for which the appropriate immediate treatment includes intravenous fluid therapy and blood transfusion, regardless of the underlying cause of blood loss. Alcohol use disorder promotes the formation of gastric and duodenal ulcers through mucosal irritation and gastritis. If an ulcer erodes through the mucosa and submucosa, marked bleeding can occur from the underlying vessels. Posterior duodenal ulcers are often associated with erosion into the gastroduodenal artery. If bleeding is not promptly addressed with fluid resuscitation, blood transfusion, and endoscopic or surgical control, rapid exsanguination and death can result. Treatment should also include administration of an intravenous proton pump inhibitor.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Intravenous administration of ADH (vasopressin) (Choice A) would not take the place of immediate fluid resuscitation and blood transfusion in a patient with blood loss, tachycardia, and hypotension. It no longer has a recognized role in the immediate management of gastritis or peptic ulcer disease. Intravenous administration of esmolol (Choice B) may worsen the hemodynamics of a patient with hemorrhagic shock and is contraindicated, as it blocks beta-adrenergic receptors resulting in decreased heart rate and myocardial contractility, which in turn decreases cardiac output. In cases of hemorrhagic shock, mean arterial pressure is maintained by systemic vascular resistance and heart rate; stroke volume is often dramatically diminished because of low preload in the setting of blood loss. Endoscopic-guided sclerosis of the esophageal varices (Choice D) is incorrect, as the patient's hemorrhagic shock is secondary to a bleeding duodenal ulcer, not esophageal varices. Any active variceal bleeding would have been noted during the upper endoscopy. Placement of a transjugular intrahepatic portal shunt (Choice E) is used in the prevention of variceal bleeding by decreasing portal venous pressure. It does not have an immediate role in the management of a bleeding duodenal ulcer. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A previously healthy 37-year-old man comes to the physician because of blurred vision for 2 weeks . His blood pressure is 130/85 mm Hg. Visual acuity is 20/20 in both eyes. Funduscopic examination shows slightly pale optic discs . Visual field testing shows bitemporal hemianopia . The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Pituitary adenoma is associated with bitemporal hemianopsia because of its proximity to the optic chiasm. The nasal (medial) retina receives light entering the eye from temporal (lateral) sources. The fibers from this area of the retina travel within the medial aspect of the optic nerve, and then cross at the optic chiasm to form the optic tract within the contralateral brain. Damage to these fibers anywhere along their course will prevent the patient from perceiving images projected on the retina from the temporal field of view. Classically, patients report poor peripheral vision and a resultant inability to walk or drive as they cannot see things lateral to their bodies. The optic chiasm sits directly superior to the sella turcica, and pituitary adenomas may grow superiorly, compressing the chiasm resulting in loss of a patient's bilateral temporal field of view.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Basilar artery aneurysms (Choice A), when small and unruptured, may be asymptomatic. In cases of rupture or thrombosis, the posterior intracranial circulation may be affected, and patients can present with headache, cranial nerve deficits, nausea, vomiting, vertigo, and ataxia. Cavernous sinus thrombosis (Choice B) classically follows an infection or injury involving a structure drained by the cavernous sinus (e.g., sinusitis), and results in cranial nerve deficits involving those that traverse the cavernous sinus (oculomotor, trochlear, trigeminal, and abducens nerves). Classic symptoms include ipsilateral orbit pain, proptosis, periorbital edema, and impairment in extraocular movement, pupil reactivity, or symmetry. Craniopharyngioma (Choice C) is a tumor seen in the sella turcica derived from remnants of Rathke pouch. It is the most common supratentorial tumor in childhood, although it is much less common than pituitary adenomas in adults. When large, they can compress the optic chiasm and cause bitemporal hemianopsia. Optic nerve glioma (Choice D) typically presents with unilateral vision loss or an afferent pupillary defect. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: While undergoing a splenectomy for immune thrombocytopenic purpura , a 49-year-old man aspirates during a difficult intubation . The diagnosis is confirmed when bile is aspirated from the trachea . Which of the following factors is most predictive of the severity of the resulting aspiration pneumonia?

choices.A: Amount of bile present in the aspirate
choices.C: Presence of solid material in the aspirate

correctExplanation: The inhalation of orogastric contents is known as aspiration, and it can occur from simple fluids such as water or stomach contents such as emesis or regurgitated products. Small volume, simple fluid aspiration may be resorbed by the lung without any consequence of infection, irritation, or compromised gas exchange. In other cases, large volume aspiration may sufficiently impair gas exchange resulting in refractory hypoxia. The aspiration of acidic stomach contents may cause aspiration pneumonitis, whereas the aspiration of gastrointestinal flora and additional bacteria can cause aspiration pneumonia. The volume of aspirate is the strongest predictor of complications from aspiration, especially in the case of pneumonia, as the bacterial inoculum may overwhelm the native ability of the pulmonary alveolar defenses (macrophages, cilia, mucus) to prevent colonization, replication, and infection. Aspiration pneumonia classically presents with cough productive of foul-smelling sputum, fever, chills, chest pain, shortness of breath, and rhonchi on examination. Imaging classically shows an infiltrate in the most dependent segments of lung at the time of aspiration (e.g., in the superior segment of the inferior lobe when supine or lower lobes when erect), and treatment includes broad-spectrum antibiotics with sufficient coverage of oral flora, gram-negative rods, and anaerobes.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Amount of bile present in the aspirate (Choice A) may be a factor in determining the severity of a noninfectious aspiration pneumonitis but would not play an immediate role in predicting the severity of an aspiration pneumonia. Duration of endotracheal intubation (Choice B) increases the risk for ventilator-associated pneumonia, which is not characteristically caused by oral flora. Typical organisms include Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Presence of solid material in the aspirate (Choice C) increases the risk for airway obstruction and atelectasis following aspiration, and also increases the risk for pneumonia, but to a lesser extent than the overall volume of aspiration fluid. Use of prophylactic antibiotics preoperatively (Choice D) is indicated to prevent skin and soft-tissue infections, contamination from the operative incision, sepsis, and peritonitis in the case of intra-abdominal surgery. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous
